citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Read consistency'
cards.answer: eventually consistent read

cards.prompt: A ___ is routed so that it only ever returns the result of all writes that completed successfully before it began — it never observes stale data, but at the cost of being routed more narrowly and being unavailable to a read request made against a global secondary index.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Read consistency'
cards.answer: strongly consistent read

cards.prompt: Why can a query against a global secondary index never be strongly consistent in DynamoDB?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Read consistency'

choices.text: A GSI's entries are propagated to it asynchronously from the base table, so there is no way to route a read that is guaranteed to have seen the very latest base-table write
GSIs do not support the ConsistentRead parameter at all in any form
Strongly consistent reads are only possible on tables without any indexes
AWS disables strong consistency to save storage costs

cards.prompt: This mirrors the standard framing of read-your-writes consistency: routing a read to the ___ (or, in DynamoDB's case, to whichever replica is authoritative for that item) is what guarantees seeing your own prior write, at the cost of that read no longer being spreadable across every replica the way a stale-tolerant read is.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Read consistency'
cards.answer: leader

cards.prompt: What is the cost of always choosing strongly consistent reads over eventually consistent ones, even though both return correct data once the system has caught up?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Read consistency'
cards.answer: A strongly consistent read must be routed more narrowly (effectively to the authoritative copy) rather than load-balanced across any available replica, and it can be refused or delayed on a partition that is temporarily unavailable — trading some of the availability and throughput headroom that eventually consistent reads get from being served by whichever replica answers fastest.

cards.prompt: Why does DynamoDB default to eventual consistency rather than strong consistency?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Read consistency'
cards.answer: Eventually consistent reads can be served by any replica, which spreads load more evenly and tolerates a temporarily unreachable replica without failing the read; most application reads can tolerate a brief staleness window, so defaulting to the more available, more distributable option and letting callers opt into strong consistency only where correctness demands it is the better tradeoff for the common case.

cards.prompt: Explain the connection between DynamoDB's eventually-consistent-by- default read mode and the read-your-writes guarantee. Why does asking for a strongly consistent read solve the same problem that routing reads to the leader solves in a single-leader replicated system?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Read consistency'

cards.prompt: A table's ___ is the only part of an item's shape that DynamoDB enforces; every other attribute is optional and can differ from item to item within the same table.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Core components of Amazon DynamoDB'
cards.answer: primary key

cards.prompt: A **composite primary key** adds a ___ alongside the partition key.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Core components of Amazon DynamoDB'
cards.answer: sort key

cards.prompt: What does a composite primary key buy you that a simple primary key cannot?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Core components of Amazon DynamoDB'
cards.answer: The ability to group a whole family of related items — an "item collection" — under one partition key value and retrieve them together, ordered, in a single request; a simple key can only ever address one item at a time by its unique value, with no built-in notion of an ordered group.

cards.prompt: A table uses a composite primary key of `(UserId, OrderDate)`. What does this let you do that a simple key on `UserId` alone would not?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Core components of Amazon DynamoDB'

choices.text: Store many orders per user and fetch them together, sorted by date, in one request
Make `UserId` values unique across the table
Avoid specifying an attribute type for `UserId`
Allow items to omit `UserId` entirely

cards.prompt: DynamoDB is schemaless below the key: an item can carry any set of non-key attributes, of any type, and two items in the same table can have completely different attributes. Only the ___ — which attributes form the primary key, and their types — is declared when the table is created and fixed thereafter.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Core components of Amazon DynamoDB'
cards.answer: key schema

cards.prompt: Why can two items in the same DynamoDB table have entirely different sets of non-key attributes?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Core components of Amazon DynamoDB'
cards.answer: Because DynamoDB validates only the primary key attributes against the table's declared key schema at write time; every other attribute is stored as part of that item's own document-like structure and is never checked against any table-wide column definition.

cards.prompt: A relational table enforces a fixed set of columns for every row. Explain what problem this creates when an application's entities have optional or varying fields, and how DynamoDB's schemaless-attributes-plus-fixed-key-schema design sidesteps it without giving up a way to address and group items reliably.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Core components of Amazon DynamoDB'

cards.prompt: Overall table throughput scales with the ___ in use, not with the capacity of any single machine — which is exactly why one partition absorbing a disproportionate share of traffic caps the whole table's effective throughput at what that one partition can push.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Partitions and data distribution'
cards.answer: number of partitions

cards.prompt: A ___ is a partition that receives a disproportionate share of a table's traffic relative to the others, because many requests hash to the same partition key value (or a small set of them) at once.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Partitions and data distribution'
cards.answer: hot partition

cards.prompt: Why does hashing the partition key not, by itself, prevent a hot partition?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Partitions and data distribution'
cards.answer: Hashing only determines *which* partition an item lands on; it does nothing about *how many* requests target that same key value. If the application's traffic itself is skewed — one popular item, a small config table, a low-cardinality status field used as the key — every one of those requests hashes to the same partition regardless of how well-distributed the hash function is.

cards.prompt: Which partition key design is most likely to create a hot partition in DynamoDB?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Partitions and data distribution'

choices.text: A status field with only a handful of possible values (e.g. "PENDING", "DONE") used as the sole partition key
A randomly generated UUID used as the sole partition key
A composite key combining a high-cardinality user ID with a timestamp sort key
A partition key value that includes a random numeric suffix

cards.prompt: This is the same failure mode key-range partitioning suffers under a monotonically increasing key — sequential IDs or timestamps concentrating writes on one range — except DynamoDB's hash partitioning trades that particular failure away only to reintroduce a version of it whenever the key values themselves have ___ or skewed access frequency.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Partitions and data distribution'
cards.answer: low cardinality

cards.prompt: What technique lets a single logical entity's traffic spread across multiple physical partitions when its natural key has too few distinct values?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Partitions and data distribution'
cards.answer: Appending a calculated suffix to the natural key — for example a random or hashed value — so requests that would otherwise all target one partition key value are distributed across several, then fanning out reads across those suffixed values and merging the results in the application.

cards.prompt: DynamoDB does absorb some of this for you. ___ is always on, needs no opt-in, and can shift throughput toward a struggling partition — even isolating a single very hot item onto a partition of its own.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Partitions and data distribution'
cards.answer: Adaptive capacity

cards.prompt: Key-range partitioning risks hot spots from sequential keys, while hash partitioning avoids that specific problem. Explain why DynamoDB's hash-based partitioning is not immune to hot partitions in general, and connect the failure mode back to the "access pattern concentrates" framing used for key-range partitioning.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Partitions and data distribution'

cards.prompt: A **Scan** operation examines ___, filtering out the ones that don't match after reading them, regardless of how few items actually satisfy the filter.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Working with queries' and 'Working with scans'
cards.answer: every item in the table

cards.prompt: Why is a DynamoDB Scan with a filter expression generally far more expensive than an equivalent Query?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Working with queries' and 'Working with scans'

choices.text: The filter is applied after DynamoDB has already read every item in the table (or index); a Query instead reads only the items within the targeted partition key's collection
Scan always returns incorrect results, while Query never does
A Scan cannot use a filter expression at all
Query is a client-side operation, while Scan runs entirely on the server

cards.prompt: Why does this push DynamoDB modeling to start from the application's access patterns rather than from the entities it stores?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Working with queries' and 'Working with scans'
cards.answer: The primary key and any secondary indexes are the only cheap entry points into the data; if you model the schema around the entities first and figure out queries afterward, you frequently end up needing to look items up by an attribute nothing was keyed on, leaving Scan as the only option — so the queries the application will actually run have to be enumerated before the key schema is chosen, not after.

cards.prompt: This inverts the modeling order a relational database encourages. A relational schema is normalized around the ___, on the assumption that a query planner and arbitrary joins can answer whatever question comes up later; DynamoDB has no query planner and no cross-partition joins, so a key schema chosen without a known query in mind is a bet that Query will happen to work, not a guarantee that it will.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Working with queries' and 'Working with scans'
cards.answer: entities and their relationships

cards.prompt: What specifically does a relational database provide that lets entity-first modeling work there, which DynamoDB lacks?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Working with queries' and 'Working with scans'
cards.answer: A query planner capable of ad-hoc joins and secondary access paths at query time, so a normalized, entity-shaped schema can still answer new questions later; DynamoDB has no join operator and no planner, so any access path not already baked into the primary key or a secondary index has no cheap route at all.

cards.prompt: This often means deliberately ___ across multiple items or attributes, so that the right value is already sitting on a key wherever an access pattern needs to look it up, rather than requiring a join or a Scan to derive it at read time.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Working with queries' and 'Working with scans'
cards.answer: duplicating data

cards.prompt: Explain why "design the table around your access patterns, not your entities" is not just DynamoDB-specific advice but a direct consequence of Query only being able to search within one partition key's item collection. What happens to an access pattern that wasn't anticipated when the table was designed?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Working with queries' and 'Working with scans'

cards.prompt: A **local secondary index (LSI)** shares its partition key with the base table and lets you choose a different sort key for querying within one partition key's item collection. It must be created at ___ and cannot be added or removed later.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Improving data access with secondary indexes'
cards.answer: table-creation time

cards.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes a GSI from an LSI?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Improving data access with secondary indexes'

choices.text: A GSI can use a partition key different from the base table's and can be created after the table already exists; an LSI must share the base table's partition key and can only be created alongside the table
An LSI can span multiple partitions while a GSI is confined to one
A GSI is always strongly consistent while an LSI is always eventually consistent
An LSI supports more attribute types than a GSI

cards.prompt: What is the practical consequence of an LSI needing to be defined at table-creation time, for a table that is already live in production?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Improving data access with secondary indexes'
cards.answer: You cannot retrofit an LSI onto an existing table to support a new access pattern — the only way to get one is to create a new table with the LSI defined upfront and migrate the data, whereas a GSI can simply be added to the live table.

cards.prompt: Why might a table designer deliberately choose a narrower projection (KEYS_ONLY or INCLUDE) over ALL for a secondary index?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Improving data access with secondary indexes'
cards.answer: A narrower projection keeps the index smaller and cheaper to store and write, at the cost of needing an extra round trip to the base table whenever a query needs an attribute the index didn't copy — it's a storage/write-cost tradeoff against read convenience, not a correctness one.

cards.prompt: The consistency difference is the sharpest distinction between the two. An LSI supports strongly consistent reads, because it is stored on the same partition as the base-table item it indexes and updated as part of the same write. A GSI, whose entries can live on entirely different partitions from the base item, is updated ___ after the base write, so a GSI query can only ever be eventually consistent.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Improving data access with secondary indexes'
cards.answer: asynchronously

cards.prompt: What causes a GSI to be eventually consistent while an LSI can be read strongly consistent?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Improving data access with secondary indexes'
cards.answer: An LSI shares its partition with the base item, so both are updated together in the same write; a GSI's entry generally lives on a different partition, reached by a separate, asynchronous propagation step after the base write completes, leaving a window where the GSI has not yet caught up.

cards.prompt: Capacity ownership follows the same split. A GSI has provisioned throughput settings ___ from the base table's, so a GSI whose capacity is exhausted can throttle its queries — and its writes — while the base table is entirely healthy.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Improving data access with secondary indexes'
cards.answer: separate

cards.prompt: A team needs a new query pattern on a table that already has significant production traffic and cannot tolerate a migration. Explain which secondary index type is even an option here, and why the other one is off the table regardless of which key structure it would ideally use.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Improving data access with secondary indexes'

cards.prompt: **Key overloading** is the technique that makes this possible: instead of a partition key meaning one fixed thing (e.g. always "user ID"), its value is a generic, prefixed string like `USER#123` or `ORDER#456`, whose meaning depends on the prefix. The ___ (commonly generic ones like `PK` and `SK`) hold semantically different kinds of values depending on which entity type occupies that item.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Best practices for designing and using partition keys'
cards.answer: same attribute names

cards.prompt: In a single-table design, what does a partition key value like `ORDER#456` typically represent?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Best practices for designing and using partition keys'

choices.text: An overloaded key encoding both the entity type (Order) and its identifier, sharing the same generic `PK` attribute other entity types also use
A composite key requiring exactly two attributes to be unique
A value that must be globally unique across every AWS account
A partition key that DynamoDB has specially reserved for order data

cards.prompt: Why does co-locating related entity types under one shared partition key value matter specifically for DynamoDB, as opposed to a relational database?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Best practices for designing and using partition keys'
cards.answer: DynamoDB has no cross-table join, so the only way to fetch related items together in one request is for them to already share a partition key (an item collection); a relational database can defer that relationship to query time via a join, so it never needs this kind of physical co-location.

cards.prompt: What is the main cost single-table design imposes on a team, compared with one table per entity type?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Best practices for designing and using partition keys'
cards.answer: The table's items are no longer self-describing or easily browsable — inspecting a raw item requires knowing the prefix conventions to decode which entity type and relationship it represents, and every access pattern must be enumerated up front since the schema is optimized tightly around them rather than left general.

cards.prompt: Single-table design is not a universal best practice; AWS's own guidance frames it as one option with real costs, not a default. It pays off when an application has a well-understood, largely fixed set of access patterns and wants to minimize the number of requests needed to serve them. It pays off less when access patterns are still evolving, when a team values being able to inspect data ad hoc, or when the entities genuinely don't share access patterns worth co-locating — in those cases ___ stay easier to reason about, and the join-avoidance benefit never gets exercised often enough to justify the added complexity.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Best practices for designing and using partition keys'
cards.answer: multiple tables

cards.prompt: A team is building the first version of a new product and isn't yet sure which queries will matter most in six months. Explain why single-table design is a riskier bet for them than it would be for a team maintaining a mature service with stable, well-enumerated access patterns.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Best practices for designing and using partition keys'

cards.prompt: What honest tradeoff does single-table design make in exchange for fetching related entities in one request?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Best practices for designing and using partition keys'
cards.answer: It sacrifices the table's readability and general-purpose flexibility — items become opaque without knowledge of the prefixing scheme, and the design is only worth it when the access patterns it was built around are already well known and unlikely to change often.

cards.prompt: The ordering guarantee Streams provides is scoped, not global: records are guaranteed to appear in the order the corresponding writes actually happened only ___, not across the whole table.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Capturing table activity with DynamoDB Streams'
cards.answer: within a single partition key

cards.prompt: If two writes happen to the same partition key in quick succession, what does DynamoDB Streams guarantee about the order a consumer sees them in?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Capturing table activity with DynamoDB Streams'

choices.text: The consumer sees them in the same order the writes actually occurred, because ordering is guaranteed per partition key
The consumer sees them in a random order, since Streams provides no ordering guarantee at all
The consumer sees them ordered globally across the entire table, matching wall-clock time across all partition keys
Streams deduplicates the two writes into a single record

cards.prompt: Why can't a Streams consumer assume that a record for item A always arrives before a causally-later record for unrelated item B, even though A was written first?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Capturing table activity with DynamoDB Streams'
cards.answer: The ordering guarantee only holds within one partition key's own stream of changes; writes to different partition keys can be processed and delivered by different shards of the stream, so there is no table-wide clock forcing B's record to wait behind A's — only two writes sharing the same partition key are guaranteed to preserve their relative order.

cards.prompt: This per-partition-key ordering is exactly what makes Streams useful for ___ patterns that need to replay one entity's history faithfully: as long as every write to a given item goes through the same partition key (true by construction, since the partition key is part of the item's own identity), a consumer processing that key's records in order sees a faithful, gap-free timeline of everything that happened to that entity.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Capturing table activity with DynamoDB Streams'
cards.answer: CDC

cards.prompt: What common CDC pattern does Streams' per-partition-key ordering make safe to build, that a global-but-unordered event feed would not?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Capturing table activity with DynamoDB Streams'
cards.answer: Maintaining a derived, materialized view or search index per entity by replaying that entity's own change history in order — for example rebuilding an aggregate or triggering a downstream workflow keyed to one item's state transitions — since out-of-order delivery for that one entity would corrupt the derived state even if every other entity's ordering was fine.

cards.prompt: Explain why a consumer that needs a strictly ordered history of a single entity's changes should design that entity's writes to share one partition key, and what specifically would go wrong for that consumer if the entity's changes were instead spread across multiple partition keys.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Capturing table activity with DynamoDB Streams'

cards.prompt: Streams records are not retained forever — a consumer that falls behind long enough can permanently miss records that age out of the stream. A CDC consumer should treat the stream as a log with a ___, not as a permanent, replayable-from-the-beginning source of truth, and design its downstream state to tolerate rebuilding from a fresh table scan if it ever falls too far behind to catch up from the stream alone.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Capturing table activity with DynamoDB Streams'
cards.answer: bounded retention window

cards.prompt: A ___ attached to a write (`PutItem`, `UpdateItem`, `DeleteItem`) makes the write fail instead of applying if that check evaluates false against the item's current state — for example, only updating an item if a version attribute still matches the value the client last read.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Managing complex workflows with transactions'
cards.answer: condition expression

cards.prompt: This is DynamoDB's building block for **optimistic concurrency control**: a client reads an item (and its version), computes a new value, then writes it back with a condition that the version hasn't changed since the read. If another writer got there first, the ___ makes the condition fail and the write is rejected, forcing the client to re-read and retry rather than silently overwriting a concurrent update.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Managing complex workflows with transactions'
cards.answer: version mismatch

cards.prompt: How does DynamoDB's conditional-write approach to optimistic concurrency detect a lost update?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Managing complex workflows with transactions'

choices.text: The write includes a condition that a version (or timestamp) attribute still matches what the client read; if a concurrent writer already changed it, the condition fails and the write is rejected
DynamoDB locks the item automatically on every read until the reader writes back
It compares the entire item byte-for-byte before every write
It relies on the client's system clock to detect concurrent writers

cards.prompt: What must the client do after a conditional write fails because its version condition didn't match?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Managing complex workflows with transactions'
cards.answer: Re-read the item to get its current state and version, recompute the intended change against that fresh state, and attempt the conditional write again — the failure is a signal to retry with fresh data, not a permanent error.

cards.prompt: What DynamoDB transactions do NOT provide, unlike the serializable isolation that is the strongest relational isolation level, is a guarantee that extends to every kind of read against the table. A single `GetItem` (or `PutItem`, `UpdateItem`, `DeleteItem`) issued concurrently by an unrelated caller does get serializable isolation against a ___ — it sees the affected items either wholly before or wholly after the transaction, never a partial result. What breaks that guarantee is a multi-item read like `Query`, `Scan`, or `BatchGetItem`: each individual item it touches is still serializable against the transaction, but the operation as a whole is only read-committed, so it can return some items from before the transaction and some from after, because it isn't executed as one atomic point-in-time snapshot.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Managing complex workflows with transactions'
cards.answer: transactional call

cards.prompt: Why is it inaccurate to describe DynamoDB transactions as giving the whole table serializable isolation?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Managing complex workflows with transactions'
cards.answer: A single standard operation (GetItem, PutItem, UpdateItem, or DeleteItem) elsewhere in the table does get serializable isolation against a concurrent transaction. The gap is at multi-item operations — a Query, Scan, or BatchGetItem/BatchWriteItem is only serializable item-by-item; taken as a whole it gets just read-committed isolation, so it can observe some items from before the transaction and others from after, which a true table-wide serializable guarantee would rule out.

cards.prompt: A team assumes that wrapping several related writes in `TransactWriteItems` means no other operation in the table can ever observe a partial result, under any circumstances. Explain precisely what guarantee they actually get, and name the kind of read that could still see an inconsistent intermediate state if it weren't itself part of a transactional read.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon DynamoDB, 'Managing complex workflows with transactions'

cards.prompt: A statement's condition uses `IpAddress` to compare `aws:SourceIp` against an allowed CIDR range. The request in question comes from a source IP not in that range. What happens to the statement?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'IAM JSON policy elements: Condition'

choices.text: The condition doesn't match, so the statement's Effect (Allow or Deny) doesn't apply to this request at all — as though the statement weren't there
The statement is treated as a Deny automatically, regardless of what its Effect actually says
The request is rejected before IAM evaluation even begins
The condition is ignored and the Effect applies anyway

cards.prompt: Why can't a policy author add an arbitrary new condition key of their own choosing?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'IAM JSON policy elements: Condition'
cards.answer: Context keys are populated by AWS itself from the details of the actual request — a condition can only compare against information the platform already knows and exposes, not information a policy author wishes were available; inventing a key that AWS doesn't populate simply never matches anything.

cards.prompt: What does the `IfExists` suffix on a condition operator (as in `StringEqualsIfExists`) change about how it evaluates a request where the named context key is missing?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'IAM JSON policy elements: Condition'
cards.answer: Without the suffix, a missing key causes the comparison to fail as a mismatch; with the suffix, the operator simply skips evaluating that key instead of treating its absence as a mismatch, so the rest of the statement isn't blocked purely because that particular request never populated the key.

cards.prompt: Conditions are where **least privilege actually gets expressed**, in a way Action and Resource alone can't reach. An Action/Resource pair says "this identity can call `s3:PutObject` on this bucket" — full stop. A condition can narrow that same grant to "only from our corporate VPN's IP range," "only if the object is being uploaded with server-side encryption," "only if MFA was present on this session," or "only before this policy's planned expiration date" — constraints that have nothing to do with which action or resource is named, and ___ to do with the circumstances under which it's acceptable.
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'IAM JSON policy elements: Condition'
cards.answer: everything

cards.prompt: A policy grants `s3:DeleteObject` with no condition at all, versus a second version of the same policy that adds a condition requiring `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent` to equal `true`. Explain concretely what capability the second version removes that the first version had, and why that removal is a meaningful move toward least privilege even though the Action and Resource elements are identical in both.
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'IAM JSON policy elements: Condition'

cards.prompt: A statement's Condition block has two separate operators: one requiring `aws:PrincipalOrgID` to equal `o-example`, and another requiring `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent` to equal `true`. A request satisfies the org-ID check but was made without MFA. Does the condition match?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'IAM JSON policy elements: Condition'

choices.text: No — multiple condition operators in the same block are combined with AND, so every one of them must match, and this request fails the MFA check
Yes, because matching either operator is enough to satisfy the block
Yes, but only the org-ID check is actually enforced
The block errors out because it isn't allowed to contain two operators

cards.prompt: A different statement uses `StringEquals` on `aws:RequestedRegion` with three values: `us-east-1`, `us-west-2`, `eu-west-1`. A request comes from `us-west-2`. Does that single operator match?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'IAM JSON policy elements: Condition'

choices.text: Yes — multiple values listed for the same key under one operator are combined with OR, so matching any one value is enough
No, because all three listed values would have to match simultaneously
No, because a single operator can only ever compare against one value
It depends on the order the values are listed in

cards.prompt: Why is it "AND across operators, OR within a single key's value list" rather than the reverse?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'IAM JSON policy elements: Condition'
cards.answer: Each distinct operator (or distinct key) expresses a separate requirement the request has to satisfy, so a statement with several of them is only as permissive as its strictest requirement — that's AND. A single key, though, can only ever hold one actual value on a given request, so listing several candidate values for it is really asking "does the request's one value match any of these" — that's OR, because the request could never match more than one of them at once anyway.

cards.prompt: Why does a Deny statement with a condition of `"aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent": "false"` behave very differently from an Allow statement with the same condition written as `"true"`, even though they sound like opposites?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'IAM JSON policy elements: Condition'
cards.answer: The Deny version blocks requests specifically when MFA was absent, leaving every MFA-authenticated request to be decided by whatever else applies; the Allow version only grants access when MFA was present and contributes nothing when it wasn't, meaning by itself it grants nothing to a non-MFA session rather than actively blocking it — the two are not mirror images once other policies are in the picture, because one actively denies and the other simply doesn't allow.

cards.prompt: **Mechanism one: role assumption.** The resource account creates a role whose trust policy names the other account (or a specific principal in it) as allowed to call `sts:AssumeRole`. Once assumed, the caller is acting entirely inside the resource account, as a session of that role — there's no "their identity policy" to separately satisfy anymore, because for the duration of the session, the ___ is the only identity policy in play. The trust-policy/ permissions-policy split this mechanism relies on is covered separately.
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Providing access to AWS accounts owned by third parties'
cards.answer: role's own permissions policy

cards.prompt: Which of these best distinguishes the two cross-account mechanisms?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Providing access to AWS accounts owned by third parties'

choices.text: Role assumption changes who the caller is acting as (inside the resource account); a resource-based policy lets the caller keep acting as themselves while the resource account grants them access directly
Role assumption is for humans, resource-based policies are only for services
They differ only in which services support each one, with no structural difference otherwise
Resource-based policies always require the caller to also assume a role first

cards.prompt: Both mechanisms still have to satisfy "both sides must allow" — they just satisfy it in different places. With role assumption, the trust policy is the resource-account side's allow (it decides who may even become the role), and the role's own permissions policy stands in for the identity-policy side, since the session has no other identity policy to consult. With a resource-based policy, the resource account's policy is the resource-side allow, and the caller's ___ in their home account must independently allow the action too — exactly the rule that makes naming an external account in a bucket policy necessary but not sufficient.
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Providing access to AWS accounts owned by third parties'
cards.answer: own, unchanged identity policy

cards.prompt: Why does an external account, once its principal is named in a bucket policy, still fail to read the object if that account never granted the action in its own identity policies?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Providing access to AWS accounts owned by third parties'
cards.answer: Naming the account in the bucket policy only satisfies the resource-account side of a cross-account request; the "both sides must allow" rule means the calling account's own identity policy still has to grant the action independently, and a bucket policy has no way to reach into another account and supply that.

cards.prompt: A team wants Account B's Lambda function to write to Account A's S3 bucket. Explain the two different ways this could be wired up (role assumption vs. a bucket policy naming Account B), and what has to exist on Account B's side either way — because "both sides must allow" applies to both mechanisms, not just one of them.
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Providing access to AWS accounts owned by third parties'

cards.prompt: What's the practical reason teams tend to prefer role assumption over resource-based policies for cross-account access that involves broad or evolving permissions?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Providing access to AWS accounts owned by third parties'
cards.answer: Role assumption produces an auditable, time-limited session with its own CloudTrail identity and an expiration built in, and the permissions granted live in one place (the role's permissions policy) rather than being split across a resource policy and a separate identity policy in another account that both have to be kept in sync.

cards.prompt: **Wildcards accumulate.** `s3:*` on `Resource: "*"` is the fastest way to unblock a developer who's hit an Access Denied, and it works every time — which is exactly the problem. Each individual wildcard grant is a rational response to an immediate blocker, but nothing about IAM prompts anyone to come back later and narrow it once the blocker is gone; the ___ of a policy under normal development pressure is to only ever get broader, never narrower, unless something deliberately intervenes.
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Grant least privilege'
cards.answer: default trajectory

cards.prompt: Why do overly broad IAM policies tend to accumulate over a project's lifetime rather than staying narrow from the start?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Grant least privilege'

choices.text: Widening a policy immediately unblocks whoever hit the denial, while narrowing one requires someone to notice the excess and deliberately do the (riskier, lower-urgency) work of tightening it
IAM policies automatically widen their own scope over time as a platform behavior
Least privilege is a theoretical ideal that AWS's own tooling actively discourages
Wildcards are required for any policy attached to a role, unlike one attached to a user

cards.prompt: Why is "grant broad access now, narrow it later" a much easier habit to fall into than to reverse?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Grant least privilege'
cards.answer: Granting broad access resolves an immediate, visible problem (a blocked developer, a failing deploy) with a one-line change; narrowing it later requires someone to first notice the excess exists, then verify narrowing it won't break something that quietly depends on it — work that's invisible until it's skipped, and easy to keep deferring because nothing forces it to happen.

cards.prompt: **IAM Access Analyzer** attacks this from the other direction: instead of guessing at the narrowest policy a role could need, it observes the role's actual CloudTrail activity over a chosen window and generates a policy scoped to the ___ — turning "what does this role need" from a manual audit of application code into an evidence-based question the platform can answer for you. Access Analyzer's policy generation is a starting point to review, not something to accept unmodified — activity logs only capture what happened to run during the observation window, not every legitimate path through the code.
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Grant least privilege'
cards.answer: actions and resources that were genuinely used

cards.prompt: Explain why a policy generated by Access Analyzer from 30 days of observed activity might be *too* narrow for a role that runs infrequent, but legitimate, code paths — a monthly batch job, an error-handling branch that's never actually been triggered. What risk does blindly adopting the generated policy carry that a more conservative "review and adjust" approach avoids?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Grant least privilege'

cards.prompt: What makes "just tighten the policy" a genuinely harder recommendation to follow than it sounds, rather than simple negligence on a team's part?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Grant least privilege'
cards.answer: Tightening requires confidence that nothing still legitimately depends on the permissions being removed, and that confidence is expensive to obtain — it needs either thorough monitoring over enough time to see rare code paths exercise their permissions, or enough test coverage to exercise them deliberately; without that confidence, narrowing a policy is a bet that something currently working keeps working, made under exactly the same time pressure that produced the wildcard in the first place.

cards.prompt: Why is "least privilege" better understood as a continuous process than a one-time policy-writing exercise?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Grant least privilege'
cards.answer: Because the forces that widen a policy (an urgent unblock) recur constantly while the forces that narrow one (a deliberate audit) don't happen on their own — treating least privilege as something achieved once at policy-authoring time ignores that the same accumulation pressure keeps acting on the policy for as long as the role exists, so only a recurring review process actually counteracts it.

cards.prompt: A **permission boundary** is an IAM policy attached to a specific user or role that sets the maximum permissions that identity's own identity policies are allowed to grant. It is evaluated as a ___, never as a source of Allow: an action is only usable if the identity policy grants it **and** the boundary also allows it. If the boundary is silent on an action (no matching Allow), that action is off-limits no matter how generously the identity policy grants it.
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Permissions boundaries for IAM identities'
AWS Organizations User Guide — 'Service control policies (SCPs)'
cards.answer: ceiling

cards.prompt: A role's identity policy grants `s3:*` on all resources. Its permission boundary allows only `s3:GetObject`. What can the role actually do?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Permissions boundaries for IAM identities'
AWS Organizations User Guide — 'Service control policies (SCPs)'

choices.text: Only `s3:GetObject` — the boundary caps the identity policy's grant down to their intersection, and it never adds anything the identity policy didn't already grant
Everything the identity policy grants, since the boundary only matters when it's more permissive
Nothing, because a boundary and an identity policy can never coexist
`s3:*`, because permission boundaries only apply to resource-based policies

cards.prompt: Why is it wrong to describe a permission boundary as "another policy that grants permissions, evaluated alongside the identity policy"?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Permissions boundaries for IAM identities'
AWS Organizations User Guide — 'Service control policies (SCPs)'
cards.answer: Because a boundary never contributes an Allow of its own — the identity's actual permissions are the intersection of what the identity policy grants and what the boundary permits, so a boundary can only remove reachable actions from what the identity policy already grants, never add any.

cards.prompt: An SCP attached to an OU denies `iam:CreateAccessKey` for every account in that OU. An account in the OU has an IAM user whose identity policy explicitly allows `iam:CreateAccessKey`. Explain what happens when that user tries to create an access key, and why the identity policy's Allow doesn't matter here at all.
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Permissions boundaries for IAM identities'
AWS Organizations User Guide — 'Service control policies (SCPs)'

cards.prompt: Permission boundaries and SCPs intersect with identity policies the same way, but at different scopes: a boundary caps one identity; an SCP caps every identity in an entire account or OU. Both compose the same way with everything else in evaluation — they never supply the Allow that policy evaluation looks for, they only shrink the ___ of actions an identity policy's Allow is even permitted to reach.
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Permissions boundaries for IAM identities'
AWS Organizations User Guide — 'Service control policies (SCPs)'
cards.answer: space

cards.prompt: An SCP attached to the organization root denies `iam:CreateUser` for every account in the org. Does this SCP block a user in the **management account** from calling `iam:CreateUser`?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Permissions boundaries for IAM identities'
AWS Organizations User Guide — 'Service control policies (SCPs)'

choices.text: No — SCPs never apply to the management account, regardless of where in the org hierarchy they're attached
Yes, because an SCP on the organization root applies to every account without exception
Only if the management account is also placed inside an OU
It depends on whether the management account has its own identity policy allowing the action

cards.prompt: Why would an organization use SCPs to deny `iam:CreateUser` account-wide, rather than trusting every team's individual identity policies to simply never grant it?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Permissions boundaries for IAM identities'
AWS Organizations User Guide — 'Service control policies (SCPs)'
cards.answer: Because identity policies are written and changed by many different people over time, and any single overly broad grant — even a temporary or accidental one — would create the access; an SCP set at the OU or organization level provides a ceiling that holds even if some individual identity policy is wrong, without requiring every policy author to get it right.

cards.prompt: What single sentence captures the relationship between an identity policy's Allow and a permission boundary or SCP that also applies?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Permissions boundaries for IAM identities'
AWS Organizations User Guide — 'Service control policies (SCPs)'
cards.answer: An identity's effective permissions are the intersection of what its identity policies grant and what every applicable boundary and SCP permits — never the union, and never something the boundary or SCP contributes on its own.

cards.prompt: The **Version** element identifies the policy language version being used (almost always the literal string `"2012-10-17"` today, since it's the version that introduced ___ support) and exists purely for AWS's own backward compatibility — it has nothing to do with your policy's revision history.
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Policies and permissions in IAM'
cards.answer: Condition

cards.prompt: A policy document has two statements: one with `"Effect": "Allow"` for `s3:GetObject`, and one with `"Effect": "Deny"` for `s3:DeleteObject`. What determines whether a `s3:PutObject` request is allowed?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Policies and permissions in IAM'

choices.text: Neither statement mentions it, so it falls to whatever the rest of policy evaluation decides — by default, implicit deny
The Allow statement, because it appears first
The Deny statement, because Deny statements take priority regardless of the action named
Both statements average out to a deny

cards.prompt: How many valid values can a statement's `Effect` element take, and what happens if it's left out entirely?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Policies and permissions in IAM'
cards.answer: Exactly two — `Allow` or `Deny`, with no third option; a statement without an explicit Effect isn't a valid statement, since every grant or restriction in IAM has to trace back to one of those two literal values.

cards.prompt: **Resource** identifies which specific AWS resource(s), by ARN, the statement covers. Some elements are conditionally required: an ___ policy (attached to a user, group, or role) never includes a `Principal` element, because the identity it's attached to already implies who the policy applies to; a resource-based policy (like an S3 bucket policy or an IAM role's trust policy) must include one, because it's attached to a resource rather than an identity and needs to say who it's granting access to.
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Policies and permissions in IAM'
cards.answer: identity-based

cards.prompt: Why does an identity-based policy never contain a `Principal` element, while a resource-based policy always does?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Policies and permissions in IAM'
cards.answer: An identity-based policy is attached directly to a user, group, or role, so the "who" is already fixed by what the policy is attached to; a resource-based policy is attached to a resource instead, which has no inherent identity of its own, so it must explicitly name the principal(s) it's granting or denying access to.

cards.prompt: A statement has `"Effect": "Deny"`, `"Action": "*"`, `"Resource": "*"`, and a `Condition` requiring `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent` to be `false`. Explain in plain language what this statement actually denies, and why writing the condition this way (rather than requiring it to be `true`) is the correct way to express "block everything unless MFA was used."
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Policies and permissions in IAM'

cards.prompt: The order is: an ___ anywhere always wins, full stop. If any applicable policy contains a Deny statement matching the request, the request is denied, regardless of how many other policies grant it. No Allow, from any policy, in any account, can override it.
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Policy evaluation logic'
cards.answer: explicit deny

cards.prompt: A request matches no Deny statement in any applicable policy, and no Allow statement either. What is the result?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Policy evaluation logic'

choices.text: Denied, by implicit deny — no policy being silent on the request ever means "allow"
Allowed, because nothing explicitly denied it
The request errors out rather than resolving either way
It depends on which account issued the request

cards.prompt: Why does an explicit Deny in a resource-based policy override an Allow that appears in the requester's own identity-based policy, given that both policies are "applicable" to the request?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Policy evaluation logic'
cards.answer: The evaluation order isn't about which policy is attached to what — it's a fixed sequence checked across every applicable policy at once: any explicit Deny anywhere is checked first and wins outright, before IAM ever looks for an Allow, so it doesn't matter which policy the Deny lives in or how permissive the identity policy is.

cards.prompt: For a **same-account** request — the caller and the resource belong to the same AWS account — a grant from ___ the identity policy or the resource-based policy is sufficient to allow the request, as long as neither side contains an explicit deny. The two policies are evaluated as alternatives that can each independently satisfy the "is there an allow" step; neither one is required to also grant the action on its own.
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Policy evaluation logic'
cards.answer: either

cards.prompt: Within a single account, an S3 bucket policy grants `s3:GetObject` to IAM role `Reader`. That role's own identity policy grants no S3 permissions at all, and neither policy contains a deny. Can `Reader` read the object?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Policy evaluation logic'

choices.text: Yes — for a same-account request, a grant from either the identity policy or the resource policy is enough, absent an explicit deny
No, because the identity policy must independently grant the action too
No, bucket policies can only grant access to principals outside the account
Yes, but only because IAM roles are exempt from needing bucket-policy grants

cards.prompt: For a **cross-account** request — the caller's account differs from the account that owns the resource — that "either side" shortcut disappears. The resource's account must grant access via its resource-based policy (naming the external account or principal), **and** the caller's own account must independently grant that action via the caller's identity policy. ___ have to allow the request; a resource-based grant alone is necessary but never sufficient once the request crosses an account boundary. Other cross-account access patterns, such as presigned URLs and role assumption, rely on this exact rule too.
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Policy evaluation logic'
cards.answer: Both sides

cards.prompt: Why does a bucket policy that names an external account as principal, on its own, never let that account's users actually read the object?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Policy evaluation logic'
cards.answer: A resource-based grant to an external account satisfies only the resource-account side of a cross-account request; the request still needs the external account's own identity policy to independently allow the same action, because "either side suffices" only holds within a single account — across accounts both sides must allow, or the implicit deny still applies.

cards.prompt: Explain, in terms of the evaluation order above, exactly what changes between a same-account and a cross-account request — not the order itself, but which set of policies has to agree before the "is there an allow" step can be satisfied. Why does adding an account boundary turn an "either side" rule into a "both sides" rule?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'Policy evaluation logic'

cards.prompt: An **IAM user** is a persistent identity, usually representing a person or a long-running application, with its own name and, optionally, its own long-lived credentials (a password, access keys). A user's ___ come entirely from the policies attached to it directly or through group membership — a user holds none of its own outside those policies.
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'IAM identities'
cards.answer: permissions

cards.prompt: **Groups** are not identities and cannot be a principal in a policy or an API call; a group is only a way to give the same permissions to many users at once, which is why you can add or remove a user from a group without touching the ___ attached to the group itself.
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'IAM identities'
cards.answer: policies

cards.prompt: Which of these can be named as the `Principal` in a resource-based policy?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'IAM identities'

choices.text: An IAM user, an IAM role, a service principal, or an account
An IAM group
Only IAM users, never roles or services
Only the account root user

cards.prompt: Why can an IAM group never appear as a `Principal` in a policy, even though it can be granted permissions?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'IAM identities'
cards.answer: A group is a container for attaching policies to users in bulk, not an identity that makes requests — at request time AWS always resolves the caller down to a user, a role session, a service, or the root user, and a group was never in that list of things that can act.

cards.prompt: It represents the ___ acting on your behalf — for example, Lambda assuming an execution role to run your function — rather than any human or application credential.
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'IAM identities'
cards.answer: service

cards.prompt: Explain why a service principal like `ec2.amazonaws.com` appearing in a role's trust policy does not, by itself, grant EC2 instances launched in your account any permissions at all. What second piece has to exist before that role actually does anything?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'IAM identities'

cards.prompt: The **root user** is the identity created when the AWS account itself was created, identified by the account's email address, and it is the one principal that can never be fully restricted by an IAM policy — some account-level actions (closing the account, changing the support plan) can ___ be performed by root, no matter what policies exist, because IAM policies attach to identities and root's authority derives from account ownership rather than from any policy at all.
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'IAM identities'
cards.answer: only

cards.prompt: What is the practical difference between "an IAM user with full administrator permissions" and "the root user," given that both can technically do almost everything?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'IAM identities'
cards.answer: An administrator's permissions are still expressed as an attached policy and can be revoked, boundaried, or denied by another policy at any time; root's authority for account-level actions doesn't come from a policy at all, so there's no IAM mechanism that can take it away — which is exactly why root should be used as rarely as possible.

cards.prompt: The **permissions policy** answers a completely different question: "once someone has become this role, what can they do?" It's an identity-based policy attached to the role, exactly like one attached to a user, and it has ___ influence over who is allowed to assume the role — that's the trust policy's job alone.
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'IAM roles'
cards.answer: no

cards.prompt: A role's trust policy allows account `111122223333` to assume it. Its permissions policy grants no S3 access at all. Someone in that account assumes the role and calls `s3:GetObject`. What happens?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'IAM roles'

choices.text: Denied — the trust policy only controls who can assume the role, not what the resulting session can do; the permissions policy still has to grant the action
Allowed, since the trust policy already vouches for that account
Denied, and the assumption itself would have failed too
Allowed, because trust policies and permissions policies are merged into one set of grants

cards.prompt: Why can a role's trust policy be completely permissive (say, trusting an entire external account) while the role itself remains harmless?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'IAM roles'
cards.answer: The trust policy only decides who is allowed to call AssumeRole and obtain a session; it grants zero API permissions on its own. Whatever that session can actually do is governed entirely by the role's separate permissions policy, so a wide-open trust policy paired with a narrow or empty permissions policy still leaves the role doing nothing.

cards.prompt: Calling `sts:AssumeRole` (or one of its variants, like `AssumeRoleWithSAML` or `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`) doesn't hand back a copy of the role's own credentials — there are none. Instead, AWS **Security Token Service** issues a fresh set of ___ credentials: an access key ID, a secret access key, and a session token, all tied to a short expiration (minutes to a few hours, depending on how the call was made) rather than existing indefinitely.
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'IAM roles'
cards.answer: temporary

cards.prompt: A developer's IAM user has broad permissions and assumes a narrowly scoped role to perform a specific task. Explain why the resulting session's permissions are the role's permissions policy, not some combination of the user's original permissions and the role's. What would go wrong operationally if assumed sessions instead kept the caller's original permissions layered on top?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'IAM roles'

cards.prompt: What does it mean that a trust policy and a permissions policy are "two distinct documents answering two distinct questions," rather than one merged access-control list on the role?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'IAM roles'
cards.answer: It means the two are evaluated at different moments and for different purposes — the trust policy is consulted once, at AssumeRole time, to decide whether the call is even allowed to happen; the permissions policy is consulted afterward, on every subsequent API call the resulting session makes, to decide what that session can do. Changing one never implicitly changes the other.

cards.prompt: Why does EC2 need an instance profile, when Lambda simply lets you attach an execution role directly to a function?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'IAM roles for Amazon EC2'

choices.text: An EC2 instance isn't itself capable of assuming a role directly; the instance profile is the container that bridges the instance to a role so its credentials can be delivered to it
Instance profiles are an older, deprecated concept EC2 keeps only for backward compatibility
Because EC2 instances can hold more than one role at a time, unlike Lambda
There's no real difference — "instance profile" is just EC2's name for an execution role

cards.prompt: Why does credential retrieval through the instance metadata service happen from an endpoint that's only reachable from inside the instance itself?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'IAM roles for Amazon EC2'
cards.answer: Restricting it to a local, non-internet-routable address means the credentials can only be fetched by code actually running on that instance, rather than by an arbitrary external caller who merely knows the instance exists — the network boundary is doing part of the access-control work that would otherwise fall entirely on IAM.

cards.prompt: This beats a ___ embedded in an environment variable, a config file, or (worse) committed to source control, on every axis that matters: the credentials the instance receives are temporary and automatically rotated by AWS well before they expire, so there's no key sitting around indefinitely for an attacker to find, copy, and reuse long after the fact; there's no manual rotation process to forget to run; and revoking access means changing the role's permissions policy or detaching the instance profile, rather than hunting down every place a static key might have been copied to.
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'IAM roles for Amazon EC2'
cards.answer: long-lived access key

cards.prompt: A team currently deploys application credentials to EC2 instances by baking an IAM user's static access key into an AMI. Explain the concrete operational risks this creates that an instance profile removes, and specifically why "temporary and auto-rotated" matters more than just "shorter" credentials would.
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'IAM roles for Amazon EC2'

cards.prompt: How does a Lambda function's execution environment obtain credentials for its execution role, compared to how an EC2 instance obtains them via the instance metadata service?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'IAM roles for Amazon EC2'
cards.answer: Lambda has AWS inject the execution role's temporary credentials directly into the execution environment at init time; an EC2 instance instead has to actively fetch its role's credentials from the local instance metadata service after an instance profile has been attached — the same underlying pattern of temporary, non-static credentials, delivered through a different mechanism.

cards.prompt: What would go wrong, from a security standpoint, if an organization decided instance profiles were unnecessary friction and instead distributed one shared long-lived IAM user's access key to every EC2 instance that needed S3 access?
citations: AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide — 'IAM roles for Amazon EC2'
cards.answer: A single compromised instance (or a single leaked key, from a log, a snapshot, or a public repo) would expose credentials usable from anywhere, for as long as that key remains active — with no automatic expiration, no way to scope revocation to just the affected instance, and no way to tell from the credential alone which instance was using it, unlike a role session, which is scoped, temporary, and attributable in CloudTrail to the specific instance profile that requested it.

cards.prompt: A cold start occurs when a request needs a ___, which happens on a function's very first invocation, after AWS reclaims an idle environment, or when scale-out needs more concurrent environments than currently exist.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda execution environment'
cards.answer: brand-new execution environment

cards.prompt: The delay a cold start adds comes entirely from work the ___ has to do before invoke can start: provisioning the microVM, initializing the runtime, and running your module-level code — none of which a warm invocation has to repeat.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda execution environment'
cards.answer: init phase

cards.prompt: Which of these is NOT part of what makes a cold start slower than a warm invocation?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda execution environment'

choices.text: The handler function's own per-request logic runs slower on a cold start
The execution environment (microVM) has to be provisioned
The runtime has to start up
Module-level initialization code has to run

cards.prompt: Why does a larger deployment package, or a runtime with a heavier startup sequence, tend to make cold starts worse?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda execution environment'
cards.answer: All of that additional code and any runtime bootstrapping has to be loaded and executed during init before the handler can run for the first time on that environment, so more bytes to fetch and more code to initialize directly lengthens the phase that a cold start puts on the request's critical path.

cards.prompt: Moving expensive setup — parsing large config, opening the first connection to a downstream service — out of the handler and into module-level code doesn't eliminate a cold start's cost; it just makes that cost visible during ___ rather than hidden inside the first invoke, which is still where a cold-started request pays for it.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda execution environment'
cards.answer: init

cards.prompt: A team notices their function's median latency is fine but their p99 is dominated by occasional multi-second spikes that correlate with traffic bursts rather than with any particular time of day. Explain the mechanism connecting bursty traffic to cold starts, given that Lambda scales out by adding new execution environments.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda execution environment'

cards.prompt: What lever, provided by the platform rather than by trimming your own code, keeps environments pre-initialized so an invocation skips init entirely?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda execution environment'
cards.answer: Provisioned concurrency, which keeps a chosen number of execution environments already initialized and idle, ready to serve an invoke immediately rather than going through init on the request's own critical path.

cards.prompt: A cold start is bounded to the environments that are actually being created; once a burst of traffic has enough warm environments to absorb it, every additional request lands on ___ instead of paying init again, which is why cold starts show up disproportionately at the start of a traffic spike rather than throughout it.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda execution environment'
cards.answer: reuse

cards.prompt: When concurrent invocations exceed the number of existing execution environments, Lambda responds by creating ___ in parallel, rather than queuing requests behind the ones already running — this is what "scaling out" means for Lambda specifically.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Managing Lambda reserved concurrency', 'Configuring provisioned concurrency'
cards.answer: additional environments

cards.prompt: Because each environment serves one invocation at a time, a function's concurrency is fundamentally an ___, not a property of the code itself; the same handler running on ten environments handles ten concurrent requests, and on one environment it handles one.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Managing Lambda reserved concurrency', 'Configuring provisioned concurrency'
cards.answer: environment count

cards.prompt: Reserved concurrency is a ___, not a target: it guarantees a function never gets starved of capacity by other functions sharing the account, but it also means that same function can never scale past the number reserved for it, no matter how much traffic arrives.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Managing Lambda reserved concurrency', 'Configuring provisioned concurrency'
cards.answer: cap

cards.prompt: What is the main functional difference between reserved and provisioned concurrency?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Managing Lambda reserved concurrency', 'Configuring provisioned concurrency'

choices.text: Reserved concurrency caps how many environments a function may use; provisioned concurrency keeps a number of environments pre-initialized and warm
Reserved concurrency pre-warms environments; provisioned concurrency caps them
They are two names for the same mechanism
Reserved concurrency only applies to asynchronous invocations

cards.prompt: Why doesn't provisioned concurrency prevent a function from ever cold-starting?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Managing Lambda reserved concurrency', 'Configuring provisioned concurrency'
cards.answer: Provisioned concurrency only pre-warms a fixed number of environments; traffic beyond that number still has to scale out onto newly created environments the normal way, and those new environments still pay the init phase on their first invocation.

cards.prompt: What happens to a request when a function is already running at its reserved concurrency limit and a new invocation arrives?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Managing Lambda reserved concurrency', 'Configuring provisioned concurrency'
cards.answer: It is throttled — Lambda rejects the invocation rather than creating another environment beyond the cap, and what the caller experiences next depends entirely on the invocation mode (an immediate error for a synchronous caller, an automatic retry for an asynchronous or poll-based one).

cards.prompt: A function shares an account-level concurrency pool with several other functions and has no reserved concurrency configured. Explain the risk this creates for that function's availability during a traffic spike on an unrelated function in the same account, and how reserved concurrency addresses it.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Managing Lambda reserved concurrency', 'Configuring provisioned concurrency'

cards.prompt: For a ___ invocation, Lambda does not retry a function error on the caller's behalf at all — the caller receives the error directly and any retry has to be code the caller itself writes.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Error handling and automatic retries in AWS Lambda', 'Configuring destinations for asynchronous invocation'
cards.answer: synchronous

cards.prompt: Why does it make sense that Lambda leaves retries to the caller for a synchronous invocation, rather than retrying internally the way it does for async?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Error handling and automatic retries in AWS Lambda', 'Configuring destinations for asynchronous invocation'
cards.answer: The caller is already there, waiting on the result, and is in the best position to decide whether retrying is safe or useful for that specific request (e.g. it may already have its own backoff and circuit-breaker logic) — Lambda retrying silently underneath a caller that is also blocked and waiting would just add latency the caller didn't ask for.

cards.prompt: For an ___ invocation, Lambda's internal event queue does retry a failed invocation automatically, without any caller involvement, before giving up and routing the event to whatever failure handling has been configured for it.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Error handling and automatic retries in AWS Lambda', 'Configuring destinations for asynchronous invocation'
cards.answer: asynchronous

cards.prompt: A function invoked asynchronously (e.g. by S3) throws an unhandled exception on every attempt. What happens to that event?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Error handling and automatic retries in AWS Lambda', 'Configuring destinations for asynchronous invocation'

choices.text: Lambda retries it automatically a limited number of times, then sends it to a configured destination or dead-letter queue if one exists
The event is dropped immediately with no retry, because S3 doesn't wait for a response
S3 itself detects the failure and re-sends the event
The function is throttled to prevent further invocations

cards.prompt: **Destinations** are the newer mechanism that supersede the DLQ pattern: they can route an event on ___ as well as on failure, to a wider set of targets (SQS, SNS, another Lambda function, or EventBridge), and they carry richer context — the invocation's response payload or error details — that a bare DLQ message does not.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Error handling and automatic retries in AWS Lambda', 'Configuring destinations for asynchronous invocation'
cards.answer: success

cards.prompt: Why can a single event's underlying operation end up applied more than once even though the platform "handled" retries correctly?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Error handling and automatic retries in AWS Lambda', 'Configuring destinations for asynchronous invocation'
cards.answer: A retry — whether Lambda's internal async retry or an SQS redelivery after a visibility timeout — re-delivers the same event to a new invocation with no knowledge of whether the previous attempt's side effects (a write, a charge, a message sent) actually completed before it failed; the platform's job is only to make sure the event isn't silently lost, not to guarantee it is processed exactly once.

cards.prompt: Explain why idempotency has to be built into the function's own logic (e.g. by checking a stored idempotency key before applying a write) rather than something Lambda's retry machinery can provide, given that retries by design re-deliver events whose prior outcome is unknown.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Error handling and automatic retries in AWS Lambda', 'Configuring destinations for asynchronous invocation'

cards.prompt: For a poll-based SQS trigger specifically, which mechanism controls whether a failed message gets redelivered, and how does that differ from an async invocation's retry behavior?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Error handling and automatic retries in AWS Lambda', 'Configuring destinations for asynchronous invocation'
cards.answer: The queue's own visibility timeout and redrive policy control redelivery — a message becomes visible again for another poll once its visibility timeout expires, and after enough failed receives (per the redrive policy) it moves to an SQS dead-letter queue; this is entirely SQS's own retry mechanism, distinct from the internal retry queue Lambda uses for asynchronous invocations.

cards.prompt: In a ___ invocation, the caller (an API Gateway request, another service calling the Invoke API directly) blocks and waits for the function to run and return a response, so the caller sees success or failure immediately and is responsible for deciding what to do next.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda invocation types', 'Using AWS Lambda with event source mappings'
cards.answer: synchronous

cards.prompt: In an ___ invocation, the caller hands the event to Lambda's internal event queue and gets an immediate acknowledgment that the event was accepted — not that it succeeded — while Lambda itself runs the function and handles retries in the background, decoupled from the caller.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda invocation types', 'Using AWS Lambda with event source mappings'
cards.answer: asynchronous

cards.prompt: Services like S3 and SNS invoke a function ___ by default; the caller (S3, SNS) never sees whether the function eventually succeeded, because it already moved on after Lambda accepted the event.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda invocation types', 'Using AWS Lambda with event source mappings'
cards.answer: asynchronously

cards.prompt: An API Gateway endpoint backed by a Lambda function times out and returns a 504 to the client. Which invocation mode is API Gateway using?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda invocation types', 'Using AWS Lambda with event source mappings'

choices.text: Synchronous — the caller is blocked waiting on the function and directly experiences the failure
Asynchronous — the caller would have already received an acknowledgment and moved on
Poll-based via an event source mapping — there is no caller to time out
It depends on the function's own configured invocation type

cards.prompt: The third mode, used for stream- and queue-based sources like Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams, and SQS, is **poll-based**: Lambda itself runs a separate component called an ___ that polls the source, batches records, and invokes the function on the service's behalf — there is no external caller at all, synchronous or otherwise.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda invocation types', 'Using AWS Lambda with event source mappings'
cards.answer: event source mapping
